title: Brooks Kerr's question: does he play piano like a guitarist?
summary: Willard relays Brooks Kerr's remark about Jones's distinctive chord approach; Jones agrees the guitar foundation carries over.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: I see. The reason -- one of the reasons I'm interested in this particularly is that -- you know Brooks Kerr (ABOMINIC), don't you? The young pianist in New York who's the Ellington specialist?
Oh, yes, I know of him.
Yeah. Well, Brooks is 25 years old and Brooks told me that he's always been fascinated by your playing.

And he said that he was talking to another pianist -- and I forget whom he said it was -- and they were talking about your particular approach to the piano and how distinctive it is and how you play -- your concepts are different than any other pianist they've ever heard, and they were trying to figure out why and how you approach chords and chord progressions, and so Brooks said,

"The closest we could come was that we had heard that Jimmy Jones used to play guitar, and we were wondering if maybe he approaches the piano as a guitarist." Now, is that possible? Does that make sense to you?
As I look back on myself, it's just transferring the notes from one instrument to another.
So you thought guitar first and you still -- well, you still approach it somewhat as --
But that had something to do with your original --

And of course the foundation is still there, you know. You never lose that. But as you grow and develop and begin to add things on and widen your scope, I think -- I don't know whether I could do it like I used to do it, now. I couldn't hold still, because I went to school and started learning more, and learning more, and learning more. Things advance, you know? You have to stay on top of it.
